new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Primary stress occurs on the first syllable of words
new_statements.citation: SIL PNG Branch (compiler; data from Michael Colburn and Bruce & Glenys Waters). 2004. Organised Phonology Data: Erima (Ogea) Language [ERI], Madang – Madang Province. Ukarumpa: SIL Papua New Guinea. 4 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 3, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' (page render saved)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., pdfinfo: Author "SIL PNG Branch", created 2004-08-19; running header "Erima (Ogea) OPD Printed: August 20, 2004"). Page 3 text layer (extracted text) and the page render both show, exactly as quoted: bold heading "Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)" followed by the single line "Primary stress occurs on the first syllable of words". Nothing else in the section; no examples, no secondary stress, no exceptions. The Syllable Patterns table that follows bolds the syllable illustrating each pattern (o.bu, ma.ta, mon.bo.na, ga.i.la, ni.rod.bo.de, ba.ga.ram, du.rii.ya), so the bold marks are pattern markers, not stress, as the first reader said; they do not bear on the rule. Read…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the initial syllable: every word carries its primary stress on its first syllable; tone and length are listed in the heading but no tonal statement is made (vowel length is phonemic per the vowel section).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word ('first syllable of words'); no statement about phrase-level accent, citation forms or the behaviour of long vowels (all vowels can be lengthened) or the rare CVC/loan syllables. Bold syllables in the Syllable Patterns table on the same page mark the pattern being illustrated (e.g. ga.i.la for V, ni.rod.bo.de for CVC), not stress, so they do not contradict the rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is headed 'Erima (Ogea) Language [ERI]' and lists the villages Erima, Balama, Dogia, Garima (Nuru family, Rai Coast) — the same variety as Glottolog ogea1238 (alt. names Erima, Nuru, Ogea; ISO eri). Colburn 1984 says his data are 'mainly based on the Erima dialect of the Erima language' and that speakers call the language Ogia; the OPD's data (Colburn; Waters & Waters) are presumably from the same Erima-village dialect. No separate dialect glottocode.
